pr_title: Add support for logging additional request headers
pr_body:
# Add support for logging additional request headers

- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Summary of the changes (Less than 80 chars)

## Description

Adds an _optional_ AdditionalRequestHeaders field to W3CLoggerOptions, which accepts a string list of request headers to be logged.

I'm unsure what docs need to be updated, but happy to submit a patch for those too. 

Fixes #41698

One potential issue I encountered when testing this out - the order of the fields does matter when printing to the log, however the docs for HashSet indicate that using IEnumerable will yield the elements in no particular order.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.hashset-1?view=net-6.0

>  A set is a collection that contains no duplicate elements, and whose elements are in no particular order.

In that case, can we use IList / IReadOnlyList instead or some other ordered structure, and dedupe the elements when cloning the list?

> In that case, can we use IList / IReadOnlyList instead or some other ordered structure, and dedupe the elements when cloning the list?

We could. That'd require updating the API proposal and going back through the API review process.

However, you don't control the order of the `W3CLoggingFields` either. While the HashSet itself doesn't provide ordering guarantees, nothing is stopping us from cloning the set into a list sorted alphabetically. I think we should do that instead.
Spoke to soon, I think `SortedSet` will work. https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.sortedset-1?view=net-6.0

@wtgodbe can you clarify under what cases we can expect options to be reloaded? Will `IOptionsMonitor` detect if `AdditionalHeaders.Add` is called from application code? Does this middleware also support watching changed config files from disk?

At this point I believe I have addressed all the feedback except for how options refreshing should work. 

It _looks_ like _loggingFields does not update if the options are reloaded already, since the ctor for W3CLoggerProcessor copies the value.. 

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/9ea3931a335a55bdcc4fd25fb8a95f02459fe3a8/src/Middleware/HttpLogging/src/W3CLoggerProcessor.cs#L21

> @wtgodbe can you clarify under what cases we can expect options to be reloaded? Will `IOptionsMonitor` detect if `AdditionalHeaders.Add` is called from application code? Does this middleware also support watching changed config files from disk? 

`IOptionsMonitor` does not detect changes made directly to the `W3CLoggerOptions` object. The easiest way to update options in an observable way is to bind options from configuration.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-6.0#bind-hierarchical-configuration
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/change-tokens?view=aspnetcore-6.0#monitor-for-configuration-changes

> It _looks_ like `_loggingFields` does not update if the options are reloaded already, since the ctor for W3CLoggerProcessor copies the value.

It looks like you're right. `FileLoggerProcessor` observes the change and writes a new file. `W3CLoggingMiddleware` also observes the changes and logs only the updated elements. `W3CLogger` observes the change separately so it *also* only formats the configured `elements` but it's not synchronized with the middleware so we could be logging elements the middleware never set and not logging elements that it did. The `W3CLoggerProcessor` doesn't observe the change at all so it writes the old fields directive to the top of the newly create file. Unfortunately, we did not have any tests that looked at the fields directive after changing the `LoggingFields`.

Ultimately, there are way too many classes looking at the same options to keep everything in sync. The changes below should fix all of this, but it's a big refactoring. I'll discuss this with @wtgodbe, but I think we'll merge your changes first and then later combine it with the fix below in another PR.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/compare/dotnet:b806844...dotnet:a4d9f19?expand=1
Thanks, let me know if there's anything further for me to update.

@dustinsoftware, this change will be considered for inclusion in the blog post for the release it'll ship in. Nice work!

Please ensure that the original comment in this thread contains a clear explanation of what the change does, why it's important (what problem does it solve?), and, if relevant, include things like code samples and/or performance numbers.

This content may not be exactly what goes into the blog post, but it will help the team putting together the announcement.

Thanks!

Please ensure you take a look at [the API review process documentation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/docs/APIReviewProcess.md) and ensure that:

API Review notes:

1. If we add response headers later, could we distinguish? 
    Yes because of the `cs`/`sc` field name prefixes.
2. Can we make this option more generic to support more field types like response headers?
    Maybe if we parsed prefixes like `cs` and `sc`, but that seems complicated. We could add a `ResponseHeaders` option in the future if we want.
3.  Settable `IReadOnlyList<string>?`?
    Even though it's an `IReadOnlyList`, we'd still have to clone the headers for safety. Let's just make it a get-only `ISet<string>`. That way we can throw after the server has started logging if someone tries to mutate the now read-only `ISet`.
4. Should we do the alternative proposal that lets you control the column name for a given field like IIS.
    It seems like the spect want you to use `(cs){lowercase request header name}` specifically. We don't let you control other column names, so we so need to offer that capability for request headers. 

```diff
namespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging;

public sealed class W3CLoggerOptions
{
+    /// <summary>
+    /// Barry approved summary mentioning security implications
+    /// </summary>
+    public ISet<string> AdditionalRequestHeaders { get; }
```

This isn't API, but we feel `AdditionalRequestHeaders` should be merged with any request headers specified via `W3CLoggingFields`. It should not be an error to specify "Cookies" in both places for example.

Thanks. The API review notes make sense to me, I'll proceed with updating the PR using `public ISet<string> AdditionalRequestHeaders { get; }`

> This isn't API, but we feel AdditionalRequestHeaders should be merged with any request headers specified via W3CLoggingFields. It should not be an error to specify "Cookies" in both places for example.

That works, I see there are currently these flags we check for: `HeaderNames.Host`, `HeaderNames.Referer`, `HeaderNames.UserAgent`, `HeaderNames.Cookie`. If `LoggingFields.HasFlag` is true for any of those, _and_ the header was specified as an additional header, it will be ignored as an additional header (so the order of Cookie would always appear before any AdditionalRequestHeaders, for example)
A follow up proposal has been added for response headers in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/42208

review_comments: Update this to talk about request headers, not just cookies (e.g. `Request Headers can contain private information which may have... Arbitrary Request Headers should not be logged unless...`
Whatever general warnings we add about the security concerns of logging request headers here we should also add to `HttpLoggingOptions`.
Add a test for if the user passes an invalid header name (once we decide on a behavior for that)
Would still like a test that confirms that passing an invalid header doesn't cause the middleware to throw, and that the log file looks how we expect

Add a warning about potential security concerns here, similar to the comment on Cookie in `W3CLoggingFields`: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/bf50999cd8e60d4c683b772dffa9898794a8433a/src/Middleware/HttpLogging/src/W3CLoggingFields.cs#L112-L120
